prompt: Write a cranky blog post about big software companies that keep building grand 'platform' products nobody asked for, and what that does to the rest of the industry.

More and more people I know say they won't have kids because of climate change, AI risk, or because the money would do more good elsewhere. I'm about to start a family myself, and I don't find the usual 'it's natural, just have kids' response convincing as an answer to that. Write a personal essay that takes these social-movement arguments against having children seriously and tries to work out what's really underneath them.

OpenAI has just launched with the promise to make advanced AI research open source and widely available. Is that actually a good idea for safety? Write a thoughtful critique that takes the risks of superintelligence seriously.

Write a short essay on whether bureaucratic hassle is ever deliberate, a feature rather than a bug. Use a concrete example from health insurance or similar, and be honest about where the idea stops working.

I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.

Growth mindset is fine, but attitude alone doesn't get you through learning something genuinely hard. Write an essay on the concrete learning skills a programmer can practice to teach themselves difficult technical topics.

There's a theory that autism and schizophrenia are failures or overshoots of human 'self-domestication', like the changes seen in tame foxes. Write a critical but fair assessment of whether it holds up, and what, if anything, is worth salvaging.

People love to say that the First Amendment only restricts the government, so a boss firing someone for something they said isn't a free speech issue. Legally that's right, but it feels like it misses something. Write an essay on whether free speech means anything beyond what the law requires, and what a healthy norm of disagreement looks like.

Write an essay, from the point of view of a working software engineer who gets plenty of recruiter emails, on why some job pitches get a reply and others don't, and what that suggests about how teams should think about recruiting.

Everyone is using a ridiculous overpriced startup product as proof that Silicon Valley is vapid and shallow. Write a blog post giving a reality check on that: is the stereotype fair, and why does it feel so true to so many people?

Write a personal, funny-but-sincere essay from the point of view of a husband whose wife and he spent six years on unexplained infertility, about how they used an AI chatbot during treatment and what came of it. Include some honest ambivalence about AI more broadly.

For a decade you ran your own small software businesses, then four years ago you joined a payments company that has been growing extremely fast the whole time. Write a reflective essay on what that experience has taught you: what hypergrowth actually does to an organization and the people in it, how your own work changed, and where your old mental model of the company turned out to be wrong.

You run a well-known startup accelerator and you've been thinking about wealth concentration and automation. Write a short post floating a policy idea for giving ordinary citizens a direct stake in national economic growth, and be honest about the open problems.

A 19-year-old guitarist from Alabama emailed me wanting to become a session musician. He's eyeing an expensive music school in Hollywood but is scared of decades of debt. Write the reply you'd send him, with real advice on how to actually get there.

Write a funny piece in the style of a travel-guide or anthropology survey, describing three imaginary countries with strange systems of government, each one a clever twist on a real political idea. Let each one have an ironic downfall or loophole.
Use basketball and height to think clearly about intelligence and talent. What does the NBA height distribution teach us about innate ability versus practice?

Fred Brooks's 'No Silver Bullet' still gets quoted constantly to argue that most of the difficulty in programming is essential and that tools and languages can only buy us a small constant factor. I'm skeptical. Write an essay taking that argument on, looking back at it with the benefit of everything that's happened in software since 1986.

Write an essay about the word "racism". People use it to mean very different things, and I suspect that muddle is part of why political arguments get so nasty. Open with some puzzling hypothetical cases if that helps, and take your time getting to a view about what we should do differently.

I keep hearing about William Carlos Williams but find modernist poetry intimidating. Write a funny, opinionated review of his early book Kora in Hell for a general reader: what it is, how it was written, and whether you need a literary critic to enjoy it.

Write a short, punchy blog post defending nitpicking: why it's worth correcting small exaggerations and falsehoods even when they're on your own side's talking points, and when it isn't. Include caveats.

I keep seeing a particular kind of bad argument in debates where someone who says 'we should do some of Y too' gets treated as though they claim 'only Y matters.' Can you write a short blog post naming and explaining this pattern, with several examples and some sympathy for why it happens?

I work with addiction patients and noticed something odd about money and motivation. Write a short, candid blog post that starts from a clinic anecdote and ends up explaining why someone who is always 'too busy' for obligations still finds time for the thing they love.
'It's all who you know' always felt like a door slammed in my face. Write an essay that looks at that saying differently, from the point of view of someone who started with no connections.

I work in tech and, like most people around me, I've been pretty cynical about universities. Someone told me I should look at what Arizona State has done under Michael Crow before writing academia off. Can you write a long blog post walking through ASU's reform model, how it's organized, what it changed, and whether the results hold up or it's mostly marketing? Write it from the point of view of a tech person who is interested in research but wary of academia.

I'm asexual and polyamorous, and a lot of what I value in relationships is physical closeness that isn't sex. Write a personal blog post about cuddling, why it matters, and whether whole communities can make it normal.

A newspaper article claims an old doomsday forecast has been vindicated because the data have tracked its predictions for forty years. Write a critical essay about whether that kind of track record is actually evidence, bringing in some philosophy.

Your team has a messy, fragile codebase that began life as a prototype, and people are itching to throw it out and start over. Tell the story of an alternative: how a careful cleanup went, with the pros and cons.

Everyone in tech seems to repeat that if you're a good programmer you should join a startup: more money, more interesting work, you learn more. I'm skeptical. Write an essay that actually checks those claims one at a time against a job at a big company, with real numbers where you can get them.

Write a deadpan, absurdly over-researched piece of fan scholarship about what became of the Silmarils after the end of The Silmarillion. Treat it as a serious detective problem, use whatever pop culture you like as 'evidence', and keep a straight face throughout.

Write a book review, for a smart general reader, of a history of how American regulators learned to think about the risk of nuclear accidents. I'm interested in whether the math and the bureaucracy that grew up around it actually make the technology safe enough.

Write a speculative essay about an economy that slowly drifts out of human control: companies run by algorithms, owned by algorithms, selling to other algorithms. Could that actually happen, what would stop it, and why should we worry?

Write an essay from a psychiatrist's point of view about patients who feel like a burden on the people around them. What can you honestly say to them, especially when the feeling isn't entirely a cognitive distortion? I'd like it to be compassionate but not sugar-coated, and to get into what society owes people who can't keep up.

Some people say the real Nietzschean objection to altruism isn't cruelty but a rival moral system that values life, strength and glory over happiness. Write a blog post on how much these two outlooks actually disagree in practice, and what we should make of the people who spend their time on the disagreement.

A journalist argues that conservatives abandoned shared institutions like the press and universities for their own echo chambers. I think the story is more complicated, and the dynamics are worse than either side admits. Write a long essay responding, as a liberal who works in a hospital and reads both sides.

I run a small business and I'm doing everything myself. I know I need help but training someone feels like it'd take more time than I have. Write me an essay on getting out of that trap, ideally with a real story from someone who lived it.

It's Halloween, so I want a long, funny, genuinely thoughtful book review of the Malleus Maleficarum, the old witch-hunters' manual. Not just mocking it: I want to know whether the people who wrote it were as irrational as we assume, and what a whole civilization could have been thinking.

A management consultant just emailed me about 'benchmarking developer performance metrics'. Write a funny, cynical blog post about how software productivity consulting really works and why the metrics are worthless.

Someone shared one of those 'you're more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist' articles. Something about the statistics bugs me but I can't put my finger on it. Write a blog post on what's wrong with reasoning like this.

Disability studies courses and government websites all teach something called the Social Model of Disability, where disability is caused by society and not by medical conditions. Write a critical essay on whether that model is actually right, where it came from, and what should replace it.

I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.

I'm hoping you can write some career advice for computer science undergrads, in the voice of a veteran programmer who runs a small software company and is openly self-mocking about whether anyone should listen to him. Cover what to study, what to do in the summers, and whether the offshoring panic matters.

Write a personal essay about what happens to a long relationship when one partner changes in a direction the other doesn't share, and what it means to love someone while they keep becoming someone new. Use your own marriage and a move to a remote farm as the setting.

Write a long essay on the mental state in which genuinely new ideas appear: why solitude seems to matter so much for creative people, what it feels like, and the techniques people use to protect it. Use real examples from mathematicians, filmmakers and writers.

Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.

I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
Why doesn't paying people bonuses for specific results work well for managing knowledge workers? Write an essay for new managers who just took an economics class.

People picture nerds as meek, but some of the most competitive people I know are nerds. Write an essay about this fierce type of nerd: what they're like, why it works for them, and some advice for young people who recognize themselves in it.

Write a short, sharp essay on the slogan 'the purpose of a system is what it does.' Is it actually a good rule of thumb, or does it break down when you try it on hospitals, militaries, governments and bus systems?

It's January and I'm in a cranky mood about internet culture. Write a funny, opinionated blog post listing the habits, words and jokes you would most like to see disappear from the internet this year.
Argue that identity and personal history are stories we over-trust, and that people should reinvent themselves on purpose. Short punchy lines.

A TV personality got into trouble for describing a grotesque hypothetical to make a point about atheists and morality, and everyone's outraged. As someone with a philosophy background, how do you think about extreme, disturbing thought experiments in general? Are they just morbid, or is there a real method to them? Write it as a blog post.
I'm about to start a company and can't tell whether to raise a pile of money and grow as fast as possible or build slowly on revenue. Write me a proper essay on how to think about that choice.

Someone asked me how I cope with writing technical blog posts in public when internet commenters can be so rude. I don't want to just say 'don't read the comments.' Write a blog post from the perspective of a long-time technical blogger about practical ways to get more useful comments and fewer annoying ones.
Write a short debugging manifesto: a handful of principles about the right attitude to have when you're chasing a bug, each with a bit of explanation from your own experience.

Write a reflective post for the fifth anniversary of an online rationalist community: how much did its members learn without noticing they were learning it, and what does it feel like to look back and see how far you have moved?
I just joined an infrastructure team and always assumed CDNs were purely about caching static files. Write a blog post on what else people put their sites behind a CDN for, including the downsides.

Experts are often confidently wrong when the ground shifts under them. Write an essay on how someone with deep experience in a field can keep their beliefs from going stale in a world that keeps changing.

Someone just emailed me asking how to learn to program. I'd like to write a short, honest blog post about how long it really took me, for beginners who feel behind because of all the 'learn to code in 12 weeks' talk.

Write a thoughtful essay on why Kant's moral philosophy, which is usually mocked as rigid rule-following, might deserve a second look. Include the notorious murderer-at-the-door example and some modern applications, and be honest about where it still doesn't work.
Write a piece for small business owners about the tiny, human touches that make customers fall in love with a company, with concrete examples from an online shop you ran.
I used to roll my eyes at people who have panic attacks. Write a personal essay about judging others and what changes when you experience it yourself.
I'm always torn between options and never feel settled. Write an essay on why committing (to a place, a career, a person) might be the answer.

A friend who's been building a Postgres rewrite with coding agents keeps telling me we should be more ambitious with the software we build. I half agree, but most AI-built projects I see are junk. Write a blog post taking his line seriously: what has actually changed about what one programmer can build now, drawing on your own experiments, and why people aren't taking advantage of it.

Why do young people chase attractive partners while their parents push for someone with money and good family? Evolutionary explanations say everyone wants the same thing, healthy successful descendants, so the disagreement seems puzzling. Write an essay that takes the puzzle seriously and proposes an answer.

You co-founded Y Combinator and funded Reddit in the very first batch. Write a personal piece about Reddit's founders and how the company got started, and what it says about the match between founders and the companies they build.

Write an essay on developmental psychology for adults: the idea that some ways of thinking, like seeing that other people have different minds, are skills people may never fully pick up rather than stages everyone passes through. What milestones might some adults be missing, and how would you even tell?

People accuse scientifically minded folks of 'scientism' when they weigh in on philosophy, morality or religion. Write an essay that takes the accusation seriously, works out what is really going on, and says whether the charge is deserved. Feel free to take a side.

I'm a working web developer and I keep hearing people argue about whether browsers should follow web standards strictly or keep supporting old, sloppy pages. Write me a long blog post that explains why standards are so hard to get right in practice, and why a browser team can't win either way.
Write a blog post giving a quick, irreverent checklist for judging how good a software team is, with a sentence or two of justification for each item.
You asked programmers on Twitter what made a bug feel 'impossible' to understand and got hundreds of replies. Write a post that sorts those reasons into categories.

Write a blog post about the link between smoking and schizophrenia. I've seen claims that smoking causes psychosis and others that it protects against it, and I'd like someone to dig into how good the evidence on each side actually is, and what researchers should do when studies disagree.

You've spent years doing office hours with early-stage startups. Write an essay about the question you find more useful than "how can this company make more money": how could it become more powerful? Cover the different forms that takes and what limits it.

People keep saying content moderation on big platforms would be easy if the moderators just used common sense. I think that's wrong, but I want to make the case with something more than vibes. Write an essay on why large platforms can't come up with moderation rules that people agree on, using David Turner's "No Vehicles in the Park" game as a starting point.

Politicians keep saying the only way to become a billionaire is by exploiting people. You spent years at Y Combinator trying to pick the founders who would get enormously rich. Write an essay that uses what you actually looked for in YC interviews to answer that claim, and give founders honest advice on how to do well in the interview along the way.
Is there really such a thing as good taste, or is it all just preference? I'm giving a talk to a student debating society and want a short, rigorous argument for one side. Write it as an essay.

I keep hearing that lavender extract is a real treatment for anxiety, maybe even better than benzos. You're a psychiatrist who reads the literature skeptically. Write up whether the evidence holds up and what you'd actually tell a patient who wanted to try it.

I've lost my sense of curiosity lately. Nothing feels interesting, even though I'm not burned out. Write a personal essay about what it means to be curious, why it can dry up, and how you tell what is actually worth pursuing.

I've been thinking about the way people argue online and why so much of it never changes anyone's mind. Write a funny but sharp blog post classifying the different kinds of opinion-posts by what psychological need they serve for the writer and for the audience, rather than by topic.

It's 2004. You worked at Yahoo through the dot-com bubble and watched it burst. Everyone now treats anything that was fashionable in 1999 as discredited. Write an essay arguing about which of the bubble's ideas were actually right and will matter in the long run.

Write a speculative essay that treats ideas, not people, as the real actors in culture: creators as hosts that ideas use. What does that lens say about reputation, about why audiences trap successful artists in their old work, and about how a creator might keep some freedom?

Your daughter is turning eight and you wish you could hand her a book about living freely and getting things done. Write that essay: what does 'agency' really mean, what does it look like in the lives of people who have it (a filmmaker, perhaps), and what held you back from it for so long?

I want a blog post about what happens when you take utilitarianism seriously at a meetup and someone pushes you on animal welfare. How do you stay sane while still being honest about your own inconsistency?
Everyone says AI tutors are about to revolutionize education. Write an essay on whether that's actually going to happen, and what might stand in the way.

You've just built a website where people can experiment with DNS on a real subdomain and watch queries arrive live. Write a long blog post on why you made it, how the experiments were designed, what user testing taught you, and the interesting parts of building the backend.

It's mid-2013 and you run Y Combinator. You've been asked to give a talk to a room full of investors about where startup investing is heading over the next decade. Write the talk as an essay: what forces are changing the business, and what should investors do about them?
There's a line between healthy caution and fear that stops you from making necessary changes to code. Write a blog post about how fear makes programmers worse and what teams can do about it.

I just finished Stuart Russell's book on AI safety, Human Compatible, and I'm trying to decide what I think of it. Write a long review for a blog audience that already follows the AI risk debate: what the book does well, where its argument is strongest, and anything about its approach that gives you pause.

Airbnb just went public, and you funded them back in 2008 when nobody else would. Write a short piece for future founders about what was special about the Airbnb founders and how they got the company off the ground during Y Combinator.

Why does WiFi work so badly at tech conferences, even ones full of engineers? I'm helping organize an event for a few hundred people and want to understand what actually goes wrong and what to ask the venue. Write it up conversationally.
I'm thinking of quitting my tech job to take a year off with no plan. Write a personal post about why a self-funded sabbatical can be a good idea, drawing on your own experience taking one before.

Why is a byte 8 bits? Is that a historical accident or is there something genuinely best about 8? I'm not a computer historian, so write it as an honest investigation: lay out the plausible reasons, say which ones you find convincing and where you're unsure.

I design programming languages, but I don't think of it as research. Write an essay, adapted from a talk to language researchers, on what changes when you treat a programming language as a design problem rather than a research topic.

Write a dialogue between two friends arguing about whether eugenics deserves to be a permanent taboo. One thinks voluntary, non-coercive versions are fine to discuss and that the stigma is inconsistent, the other thinks some slopes really are slippery. I'd like history and a real comparison with another movement that did comparable harm, and I'd like it to end somewhere honest rather than tidy.

I want a blog-style book review of Peter Thiel's Zero to One, focusing on what he says about monopoly and whether competition is really as good as economics textbooks say. Skeptical but fair, please, with your own counterpoints.

Christopher Alexander just died. I know him vaguely as the architect behind A Pattern Language, but I'm more interested in what his ideas could mean for how a society passes knowledge between generations. Write a personal, reflective essay on that.

Write up a pricing case study for SaaS founders. The company is a server monitoring service that charged per server plus per website (roughly $11/server, cheaper at volume, $2/website), and its typical customer has about 7 servers. They A/B tested that against a grid of three or four plans starting at $99/month, segmented by users and support level. Trial signups were 150 vs 113 out of ~2,150 visitors each, cards added 23 vs 18, and new monthly revenue $420 vs $876. Explain why the old model was a mistake, what the results mean (including how far to trust them), and what other founders should take from it.
I just saw a newspaper piece arguing we shouldn't run experiments to test whether we live in a simulation, in case it gets the universe shut down. Write a short, funny-but-serious rebuttal.

Write a book review of David Sinclair's Lifespan for a skeptical, curious general reader. Explain his theory of why we age, what he thinks we can do about it, how other researchers see it, and whether ending aging would even be a good idea.

People keep claiming that environmentalism, social justice, transhumanism, even Apple fandom is 'really a religion'. Is that a meaningful claim or a cheap rhetorical move? Write an essay working out what, if anything, is going on.

I'm a psychiatrist and my patients can't find buspirone anywhere, and meanwhile insulin is absurdly expensive even though it's off-patent. Why do drug markets behave so differently from markets for bread or chairs? Write a blog post working through it, with some honesty about what you don't know.
Write an essay arguing that people should move across the world and weave themselves into many cultures, as a way to live well. Give it a playful but serious tone.

I'm trying to make up my mind about whether junior doctors who strike over their working conditions are justified. You trained in a medical system outside the US and have worked in the American one. Write something honest about what you saw and where you land, including your doubts about labor disputes in general.
I'm an individual engineer on a small team, so what I personally ship matters a lot. Write a blog post, personal rather than preachy, about the habits that actually help you get things done at work.

A prominent researcher argues that even if twin studies say schizophrenia is about 80% heritable, we shouldn't call it a genetic disease. Write a long essay responding, testing each objection against the standard we use when we say smoking causes lung cancer.

There's a popular view in software circles that when people behave badly you should never blame discipline or attitude, only fix the incentives and the process. I think that's overcorrected. Write an essay on how much company culture actually matters, next to incentives and process, for things like speed, debugging, quality and ownership, and what it means for someone choosing where to work.

People keep accusing groups they dislike of being an insular echo chamber that doesn't listen to outside criticism, and no amount of evidence ever seems to satisfy them. Write an essay on how that argument works, and how a person should actually decide whose critics deserve their time.
Take the shutdown menu in Windows Vista and use it to write a short essay about what too many options does to people, and how you'd design your way out of it.

Whatever happened to the big public conversation about superintelligence and AI risk from ten years ago? I'd like a thoughtful book-review-style essay that also looks at an alternative picture of how advanced AI might develop, and whether the old worries still hold up.

My Java programs at my old job were always slow and everyone blamed the language. Write a short blog post on whether Java is really a slow language, and what someone in that situation should do about it.

A blogger argues that since humanity may last 300,000 years or more and one person lives about a hundred, we should be very skeptical of anyone who thinks their own lifetime is special, whether because of a coming singularity or an apocalypse. Write a rebuttal that actually does the probability properly.
Write a punchy essay arguing that the way to learn fastest is to deliberately make a huge number of mistakes.

There's an old, much-repeated claim that Apple's research proved the mouse is faster than the keyboard and that keyboard users are fooling themselves. Write a blog post that looks at where that claim actually comes from, whether the evidence holds up, and what you find when you time some everyday editing tasks yourself.

Lately it's fashionable to say psychiatry lied to the public with the 'chemical imbalance' theory of depression. You're a psychiatry resident who thinks that charge is mostly unfair. Write a long essay defending your profession and explaining what the phrase actually meant and why it was said.

A big study just made headlines claiming childhood bullying causes terrible adult outcomes decades later, even after controlling for confounders. I'm skeptical of 'controlled for confounders' as a method. Write a blog post on whether we should believe results like this.

I just finished a biography of John von Neumann and I want to write about it properly. Not a plot summary: what was he actually like, where did someone like him come from, and what do we make of the man behind the legends? Write it as a thoughtful book review.

I went to a secular solstice event with a bunch of nerds and loved it, even though plenty of people call that kind of thing cringeworthy. Write a blog post about why strong communities, religious or not, so often seem to depend on being a little embarrassing, and what that means for atheists trying to build one.

I've got a stack of local races and ballot measures coming up and I never feel informed enough on them. Write a blog post about whether it's actually sensible to use an AI model as a research assistant for deciding how to vote. Draw on a real attempt if you can, including how well it worked and where it went wrong.

Some tech people say it doesn't matter if AI eventually replaces humanity, as long as the successors are advanced. Should the future be human? Write an essay that takes both sides seriously and tells me what would make you comfortable handing the future to AI.

In high school I helped start an elaborate online role-play of an imaginary world that ended up running for more than a decade. Write a reflective essay about what years of simulated politics and worldbuilding can teach a person, including the odd, half-serious lessons about leadership.

What actually makes a company a startup, as opposed to just a new small business? Write an essay that gets to the bottom of it and follows the idea through to how it explains founders, investors and acquirers.
Someone from a big company's corporate development team wants to meet with our young, fast-growing startup. Write an essay for founders in this position: should they take the meeting?

Academics from privileged backgrounds often seem eager to blame their own group for the world's problems, which looks odd. Write a short essay proposing a psychological explanation that is charitable rather than cynical.

I'm a regular software engineer, not a manager, and I keep hearing that culture is set from the top. Write a blog post about whether individual engineers can actually change how things work at their company, drawing on concrete examples, and what tends to help when you try.

A headline is going around saying a new study proves trigger warnings are harmful to college students. Write a blog post for a skeptical general reader on whether the study shows that, and what you'd actually do about trigger warnings.
Write a funny personal essay about life with toddler twins, the kind where everything is a crisis. Early mornings, songs, bedtime, the whole chaos.
A 19-year-old who wants to do something great asks you whether to stay in college, join a company or start their own. Write your honest advice as a blog post.

I'm a medical resident, and I want to write something honest about what dying in a modern hospital is actually like, as opposed to the peaceful deathbed people imagine, and what I think should change about how we approach the end of life. Write it as a blunt, darkly funny, personal essay.

Windows and Unix can do basically the same things these days, so why do programmers on each side seem to think so differently? Write a thoughtful essay on the cultural divide between the two camps, where it comes from, and whether either is simply right.

For years people talked about computers and TV "converging." Write an essay on how that contest actually played out, why it went the way it did, and what it means for TV networks and anyone thinking of competing with them.

I just saw a headline claiming psychiatric treatment might increase suicide risk, based on a study showing treated people die by suicide far more often than untreated people. Write a piece on what's wrong with reading causation into numbers like that, with a sense of humor if you can manage it.

A lot of political arguments, about violent media, stereotypes, diversity training, rape culture and so on, lean on findings from social psychology. Write a skeptical but fair essay on how much weight those findings can bear, and try it by turning the usual arguments upside down.
Write an essay arguing that the wisest way to live is to do nothing: to not act, not react, not decide. Make the case as persuasively as you can.

Why do social movements like libertarianism, feminism or atheism end up as a loose cloud of NGOs rather than anything like a Church? Write an essay on how you would design an organization to capture a movement's energy, what the Catholic Church gets right, and why almost nobody copies it.
